# Hepatic infarction

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the liver > Hepatic infarction*

[Original Article Link](/library/-w0DlR)

---

## Summary

Hepatic <u>infarction</u> is an <u>ischemic</u> injury affecting two or more <u>liver</u> lobules. It is extremely rare due to the protective effect of the dual blood supply in the <u>liver</u>. For hepatic <u>infarction</u> to occur, blood flow is typically impaired in both the hepatic <u>artery</u> and <u>portal vein</u>. Etiologies include local causes (e.g., <u>portal vein thrombosis</u>, trauma, <u>liver transplantation</u>) and systemic conditions (e.g., <u>sepsis</u>, <u>HELLP syndrome</u>, <u>sickle cell disease</u>). Clinical features include sudden upper abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>fever</u>, and <u>jaundice</u>. <u>Elevated liver enzymes</u> and an elevated <u>white blood cell count</u> support the diagnosis. Abdominal imaging (e.g., <u>duplex US</u>, CT abdomen) shows a wedge-shaped abnormal area and impaired blood vessel flow. Management focuses on treating the underlying cause. Complications can be severe and include <u>liver</u> failure, <u>ascites</u>, infection, and <u>bile</u> duct <u>necrosis</u>.




For hepatic injury due to <u>hypoperfusion</u>, see "<u>Ischemic hepatitis</u>."
